7.0.big: Plants store the sun's energy in glucose. Cellular respiration is how every living thing gets that energy back out, as ATP the cell can use.
points: Like a power plant turning heat into electricity, cells turn the energy in glucose into a form they can actually use (ATP).
Glycolysis is the first step, and almost every organism on Earth does it.
Block one key glycolysis enzyme (pyruvate kinase) and the organism dies. Scientists use this to target parasites that cause deadly diseases.

7.1.big: Energy moves through cells by passing electrons from one molecule to another (redox reactions), and it gets stored in ATP, a rechargeable battery.
points: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain. The molecule that loses electrons loses energy, and the one that gains them gains energy.
NAD+ and FAD are electron taxis. They pick up high-energy electrons (becoming NADH and FADH2) and drop them off later to make ATP.
ATP → ADP + P<sub>i</sub> releases energy. ADP + P<sub>i</sub> → ATP stores it again, like recharging a battery.

ATP gets made two ways. Substrate-level phosphorylation moves a phosphate straight onto ADP and makes only a little ATP. Oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis in the mitochondria) makes about 90% of it.

7.2.big: Glycolysis splits one glucose (6 carbons) into two pyruvate (3 carbons each), in the cytoplasm, without needing oxygen.
points: First half (investment): spend 2 ATP to add phosphates to glucose, which traps it in the cell and makes it ready to split in two.
Second half (payoff): make 4 ATP and 2 NADH.
Net result per glucose: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate.
Phosphofructokinase is the main control valve. When ATP is plentiful it slows glycolysis down.
Glycolysis needs NAD<sup>+</sup> to keep going, so NADH has to be recycled back to NAD<sup>+</sup>, either by the electron transport chain or by fermentation.
Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so glycolysis is their only source of ATP.
7.2.tip: Think of it like investing: put in 2 ATP, get back 4, keep a profit of 2.

7.3.big: If oxygen is around, pyruvate goes into the mitochondria, becomes acetyl CoA, and gets fully broken down to CO2 in the citric acid (Krebs) cycle, filling up lots of electron taxis.
points: Pyruvate → acetyl CoA: one CO2 comes off and one NADH is made (per pyruvate).
Citric acid cycle (in the mitochondrial matrix): acetyl (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C). The cycle then gives off 2 CO2 and rebuilds oxaloacetate to start again.
Each turn makes 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 ATP (or GTP). Glucose gives two pyruvate, so the cycle turns twice per glucose.
By the end, all 6 carbons of the original glucose have left as CO<sub>2</sub>. That's the CO<sub>2</sub> you breathe out.
The cycle makes very little ATP directly. Its real job is loading NADH and FADH<sub>2</sub> for the next stage.
7.3.tip: Count the carbons: glucose (6) → 2 pyruvate (3 + 3) → 2 acetyl (2 + 2) plus 2 CO<sub>2</sub> → 4 more CO<sub>2</sub> in the cycle. 6 in, 6 out.

7.4.big: The electron transport chain uses the electrons from NADH and FADH2 to pump H+ across a membrane. Then H+ rushes back through ATP synthase, which makes most of the cell's ATP.
points: The chain is a relay of proteins (complexes I–IV) in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons pass down it, releasing a little energy at each step.
That energy pumps H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building up a gradient, like water behind a dam.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor: it grabs the electrons at the end and combines with H+ to make water. No O2 means the chain backs up and stops.
Chemiosmosis: H+ flows back through ATP synthase, which spins like a turbine and makes ATP from ADP + Pi.
FADH2 skips complex I, so it pumps fewer H+ and makes less ATP than NADH. All together, one glucose gives about 36–38 ATP.
Cyanide blocks the end of the chain. DNP pokes holes so H<sup>+</sup> leaks back without making ATP. Either way, ATP production crashes.

7.5.big: Without oxygen, cells still need to recycle NADH back to NAD+ so glycolysis can keep making its 2 ATP. Fermentation does that.
points: Anaerobic respiration (some bacteria and archaea) still uses an electron transport chain, but the last electron acceptor is something inorganic other than O2, like sulfate or CO2 (methanogens make methane).
Fermentation uses an organic molecule as the last electron acceptor, and only glycolysis makes ATP (2 per glucose).
Lactic acid fermentation (your muscles when they run low on oxygen, red blood cells, yogurt bacteria): pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD+.
Alcohol fermentation (yeast): pyruvate → CO2 + acetaldehyde → ethanol, recycling NAD+. The CO2 is what makes bread rise.
Facultative anaerobes can switch between respiration and fermentation. Obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen.

7.6.big: It isn't only glucose. Carbs, proteins and fats all feed into glycolysis and the citric acid cycle at different entry points.
points: Other sugars and glycogen get converted into glycolysis intermediates (glycogen → glucose-1-phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate).
Proteins: amino acids lose their amino group (which becomes ammonia, then urea in your pee). Their carbon skeletons enter glycolysis or the citric acid cycle.
Fats: glycerol enters glycolysis. Fatty acids are chopped into 2-carbon acetyl groups by beta-oxidation and enter as acetyl CoA.
These pathways are "porous": molecules come in from other pathways and intermediates leave to build other things.
In evolution, glycolysis came first, then early (anoxygenic) photosynthesis, then oxygen-producing photosynthesis. The citric acid cycle and the full ETC came after that.

7.7.big: Cells don't run respiration full-blast all the time. Key enzymes speed up or slow down based on how much energy the cell already has.
points: The usual signal: lots of ATP (or NADH) means slow down, and lots of ADP or AMP means speed up. This is negative feedback.
Phosphofructokinase is the main control point of glycolysis. High ATP, high citrate or low pH turn it down.
Hexokinase and pyruvate kinase are also controlled, and so are the citric acid cycle enzymes that make the first NADH.
The electron transport chain speeds up when ADP builds up (ATP is being used) and slows down when ATP piles up.
Glucose entry itself is controlled. For example, insulin brings GLUT4 transporters to the cell surface.

1.why: ATP is the cell's main energy currency. ADP and AMP are what's left after ATP gives up phosphates.

2.why: Reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG). When a chemical is reduced, an electron is added to it.

3.why: Oxidizing agents accept electrons. FAD and NAD+ are the empty electron taxis. FADH2 and NADH are already full, so they're reducing agents.

4.why: ATP + H2O → ADP + phosphate is ATP hydrolysis, which releases energy. The others add phosphates, which takes energy.

5.why: The second half of glycolysis is the payoff: it produces ATP (4) and NADH. The first half uses ATP and splits the sugar.

6.why: Hexokinase uses ATP to put a phosphate on glucose. The charged (polar) phosphate can't cross the oily middle of the membrane, so glucose is trapped inside.

7.why: Invest 2 ATP in the first half, get 4 ATP back in the second half, for a net gain of 2.

8.why: A carboxyl group comes off pyruvate as CO2, leaving the 2-carbon acetyl group.

9.why: NADH carries those electrons to the electron transport chain, where they're used to make most of the ATP.

10.why: The step from succinyl CoA to succinate makes GTP (or ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation.

11.why: Each turn makes 3 NADH, plus 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP/GTP.

12.why: NADH hands its electrons to complex I, which contains FMN (flavin mononucleotide). From there they go to ubiquinone (Q).

13.why: In chemiosmosis, hydrogen ions (H+), not whole atoms, flow across the inner mitochondrial membrane through ATP synthase.

14.why: As electrons move down the chain, their energy powers the pumps that push H+ across the membrane. Oxygen is reduced at the end, not oxidized.

15.why: If H+ could leak back in anywhere, there'd be no flow through ATP synthase and no gradient to use, so no ATP would be made by chemiosmosis.

16.why: Your muscles use lactic acid fermentation when they run low on oxygen.

17.why: Glycolysis makes pyruvate and NADH. Fermentation uses both: NADH hands its electrons to pyruvate (or something made from it) to get NAD+ back.

18.why: Yeast turn pyruvate into ethanol, recycling NADH back to NAD+. CO2 is given off too.

19.why: Hexokinase adds a phosphate to glucose, making glucose-6-phosphate.

20.why: Beta-oxidation breaks fatty acids into 2-carbon acetyl groups that enter the citric acid cycle as acetyl CoA.

21.why: That's the false one. Carbohydrates feed into glycolysis, not straight into oxidative phosphorylation. The other three are true.

22.why: High ATP means the cell has plenty, so it slows down glycolysis enzymes like phosphofructokinase (negative feedback).

23.why: Phosphofructokinase is the main control valve of glycolysis.

24.why: High ATP slows pyruvate kinase (ATP is a negative regulator), so increased pyruvate kinase activity is the one that does not happen. The other three do.

25.why: ATP is a standard energy packet: every reaction can use the same "coin". If cells pulled energy straight from different carbohydrates, every reaction would need its own setup.

26.why: NAD+ is an oxidizing agent: it accepts electrons (and a proton) from food molecules and becomes NADH.

27.why: RH loses electrons, so it's the reducing agent. NAD+ gains them, so it's the oxidizing agent. The products are NADH and R.

28.why: Something found in nearly every organism most likely came from a common ancestor long ago. It's very unlikely to have evolved separately many times.

29.why: Every cell needs energy for basic jobs like running the Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> pump. Red blood cells get ATP only from glycolysis, so blocking it would wreck their ion balance and they would die.

30.why: In a circular pathway like the citric acid cycle, the last product (oxaloacetate) is also what starts the next turn. A linear pathway starts and ends with different molecules.

31.why: The first step of pyruvate oxidation removes a carboxyl group, which leaves as CO2. The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex does it.

32.why: In order: (1) remove a carboxyl group, releasing CO<sub>2</sub>; (2) oxidize the leftover group to acetyl, making NADH; (3) attach the acetyl group to CoA, making acetyl CoA.

33.why: Ubiquinone (Q) and cytochrome c are mobile carriers that shuttle electrons between complexes. The big complexes stay fixed in the inner membrane.

34.why: NADH made in glycolysis can't easily get into the mitochondria, so its electrons are shuttled in, sometimes onto FAD, which makes fewer ATP. That's one reason the total varies.

35.why: Complex IV holds oxygen between iron and copper ions. The electrons end up on oxygen, which picks up H<sup>+</sup> to form water.

36.why: Fermentation uses only glycolysis and hands its electrons to an organic molecule. Anaerobic respiration uses the full pathway with an ETC but ends with an inorganic acceptor that isn't O2.

37.why: This is a methanogen: NADH's electrons end up on CO2, an inorganic molecule, making methane. No oxygen is used, so it's anaerobic respiration.

38.why: They're economical: feedback inhibition stops the cell making what it doesn't need, and intermediates get reused by other pathways.

39.why: The book names cholesterol and triglycerides as the lipids tied to glucose pathways. Glycerol (from triglycerides) becomes glycerol-3-phosphate and enters glycolysis.

40.why: When citrate or ATP builds up, it slows phosphofructokinase, so they're negative regulators. The cell already has enough.

41.why: Negative feedback brings things back to normal (homeostasis). Positive feedback pushes things further and further away, so it's only useful in special cases.

42.why: The setup measures a drop in gas volume as oxygen is used. But the animals breathe out CO2, which would fill that space back in, so you need something that absorbs the CO2.

43.why: Mice are warm-blooded: in the cold they burn more fuel (and oxygen) to make heat. Crickets are cold-blooded: cold slows their metabolism, so they use less.

44.why: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol (cytoplasm) in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

45.why: An obligate anaerobe can't use oxygen, but almost everything does glycolysis, which doesn't need oxygen.

46.why: Being found in all three domains, working without oxygen, and happening in the cytosol (no mitochondria needed) all point to a very old pathway.

47.why: This is the electron transport chain, which sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane of eukaryotes.

48.why: Structure Z is cytochrome c, which carries electrons from complex III to complex IV. Block it and that handoff stops.

49.why: Electrons come from NADH and FADH2 and end up on oxygen, which becomes water.

50.why: Glycolysis → oxidation of pyruvate → citric acid cycle → oxidative phosphorylation.

51.why: These are different organisms using different metabolic tricks for the same problem, surviving the cold: one changes its membrane fats, the other makes antifreeze proteins.

52.why: This is the whole chain in order: glycolysis → pyruvate → acetyl CoA → citric acid cycle → NADH/FADH<sub>2</sub> → ETC pumps protons → ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), together called oxidative phosphorylation.
